Why Make a Poster?

A poster does work a paper can't — it moves fast, and it starts conversations.

Reach & attention

A poster conveys a lot of information quickly to an audience wider than the people who would read your paper. Humans are visual — a strong poster stops someone mid-aisle.

Conversation

Posters are built for discussion. The people who stop are the people interested in your question — and that's where future collaborations start.

Credit

Posters and their abstracts can be published and cited. It's a citable output while a longer paper is still in progress.

Timeliness

Share preliminary data and your most current results. A poster is an evolving reflection of a study, and often the precursor to a published paper.

Choosing the Right Poster Design

Decide this first — it determines your sections, your layout, and how you'll use images throughout.

Not every poster tells the same kind of story, and the right layout depends on what kind of work you're presenting.

Empirical Research

Built on data you collected or analyzed — quantitative or qualitative. Follows the IMRaD spine: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion.

Non-Empirical Research

Social science & humanities work built on documents, images, or a central argument rather than quantitative data. Choose from Modified IMRaD, Thematic, Narrative, or Q&A.

Experiential Activities

Internships, study abroad, and other lived experience. Structure: Introduction, Purpose, Experience, Reflection, Conclusion — built around photos.

The IMRaD Spine

The standard structure for empirical and scientific posters — and a reasonable default for social science.

Sections, in order

  • Title
  • Author information
  • Abstract
  • Introduction
  • Methods
  • Results
  • and Discussion / Conclusion
  • References
  • Acknowledgments

How to weight it

Introduction and Methods should be the shortest sections on the poster. Results and Discussion earn the real estate — that's what people stopped to see.

Social sciences: you can follow this structure, but you are not required to. If your research isn't quantitative, the humanities and social science layouts a few slides ahead will serve you better.

Common IMRaD Arrangements

Same sections, three ways to divide the space. Pick the one that matches how much you have to show.

TITLE · AUTHORS · AFFILIATION
Abstract
Introduction
Methods
Results — figure
Results — figure
Discussion / Conclusion
References
Acknowledgments

Classic three-column. The safe default. Balanced, prints well at almost any size, and reads in the order people expect.

TITLE · AUTHORS · AFFILIATION
Abstract
Introduction
Methods
Methods diagram
Results — figure
Results — figure
Results — table
Discussion / Conclusion
References & Acknowledgments

Four-column, wide format. For landscape boards and data-heavy work. Narrower columns mean shorter lines — easier to read standing up.

TITLE STATES THE FINDING
Introduction
Methods
References
Results — one dominant figure
Conclusion

Results-forward. One finding, one big figure, supporting detail pushed to a narrow left column. Effective when a single result is the whole story.

Whichever you choose: Introduction and Methods should be the smallest blocks on the poster, and reading order should be obvious without arrows or numbers. If you need to tell people where to start, the layout isn't working yet.

Humanities & Social Science Layouts

There is no single required style. Pick the structure that matches your argument. On the LibGuide, this track — work built on documents, images, or a central argument rather than data — is called Non-Empirical Research Layout.

Modified IMRaD

Keep the familiar spine but add or delete sections as needed. Works when your methods are similar to science but your data isn't quantitative.

Thematic

Group the poster into sub-themes rather than research stages. Best for comparison, or when your work breaks naturally into three or four main points.

Narrative

Tell the story of your topic in paragraph form. Suited to formal analysis, discursive research, and work centered on a specific event, person, or period.

Questions & Answers

State your main research questions and show how you answered each. Direct, easy to skim, and a good fit for a poster session where you'll be talking anyway.

Because humanities and social science research is often interdisciplinary, you'll see more artistically inclined — and some genuinely abstract — posters from these fields. That's allowed.

Naming Your Sections

Humanities and social science posters have no default headings — which means yours can do real work. Three examples:

Oral history project · narrative

  • Why these voices, now?
  • Who I talked to, and how
  • What they said that I didn't expect
  • What it changes about the record

Comparative policy analysis · thematic

  • Three cities, one policy
  • Theme 1 — how it's enforced
  • Theme 2 — how it's funded
  • Theme 3 — who it reaches
  • What the comparison shows

Archival & visual culture study · questions

  • What did these images promise?
  • Who was allowed to look?
  • What survives in the archive — and what doesn't?
  • Why it matters now

The test

Read only your headings, in order, and nothing else. If someone can get your argument from that alone, the poster will work. If the headings are "Introduction, Background, Analysis, Conclusion," they're labels, not an argument.

A caution: clever headings still have to be scannable. Keep them short, keep them parallel with each other, and make sure a reader can tell at a glance which block is the conclusion.

Your Experience as Inquiry

An internship poster and a research poster are doing the same work: you started with questions, you went and found things out, and now you're reporting back.

Hands-on experience is the point

One of the major benefits of an internship is the opportunity for hands-on experience in an area you find interesting — the chance to see how a field actually operates from the inside, rather than from a syllabus.

It prepares you — and it tests a hypothesis

That hands-on experience not only prepares you for future opportunities, it also allows you to consider whether you enjoy a particular kind of work. Finding out that a field isn't for you is a real result, and it's worth reporting.

Three questions to answer before you draft

  • What questions did you have as you began your internship?
  • Which of those questions were answered?
  • Which will require further research or experience to answer?

Keep your answers. The first question usually becomes your Purpose section, the second becomes Reflection, and the third gives you a genuine closing move — the same "future directions" note an empirical poster ends on. It also gives you something to say when a visitor asks what you'd do next.

Experiential Activities Posters

Internships, study abroad, and other experiential learning are often presented this way — check whether your conference allows it. On the LibGuide, this track is called Experiential Activities Layout.

SectionWhat goes in it
IntroductionFour to five sentences summarizing the experience, ending with the goal of it.
PurposeExpand on that goal. Why this experience, and why now?
ExperienceWhat you actually did. How you spent your time, and any products or deliverables you're proud of.
ReflectionWhat you learned — new skills, insight into the field, how it shaped your career goals.
ConclusionPull the main points together. Add acknowledgments if there are people or supporters to thank.

Empirical, for comparison

Introduction → Methods → Results → Discussion / Conclusion → Acknowledgements. Same poster size, same design rules, different spine.

Use your photos

Photos from the experience illustrate your work, vary the layout, and draw people in. They also recycle straight into a LinkedIn post celebrating what you did.

Career Readiness Competencies

Your poster is also a professional document. Naming what you built and practiced makes it legible to employers.

The National Association of Colleges and Employers has defined eight career readiness competencies that employers seek out when hiring: NACE Career Competencies.

What to do with them

As you create your draft poster, consider how you demonstrated or grew in 2–3 of the listed competencies during your experience. Take a look at the sample behaviors listed for each one to see validated examples of how employers have seen these competencies put into practice.

Where this lands on the poster. Most of it belongs in Experience and Reflection. Name the competency, then give the evidence — the specific thing you did that shows it. A competency with no example behind it reads as filler; an example with the competency named is what a recruiter can repeat back to a hiring manager.

Put a Competency Into Words

Pick three competencies. In each box, write a sentence or bullet you can include in your poster describing how you put that competency into practice.

1

Start with the task, not the trait: "I …" and then what you actually did.

2

Include scale or outcome where you can — how many, how often, what changed.

3

Growth counts too — something you couldn't do in week one and could by the end.

These sentences go straight into the Experience and Reflection sections of your draft — and into the outline on the last slide.

Poster Design Essentials

The core dos and don'ts for content, text, and color. Tap a section to open it.

What Makes a Good Poster ▾
  • A visual, brief summary of the research — not a paper on a wall
  • Tables and figures carry the key elements and results
  • Legible from three feet away
  • Good contrast between text and background
  • Clear title, labels, and organizational structure
  • An easy, quick read — the gist lands in about two minutes
  • Contact information for you and your research team

The three-foot rule

Step back three feet from your screen at 100% zoom. If you can't read the body text or tell the sections apart, neither can someone standing in front of your poster.

Browse a few real posters before you design anything — you'll learn more in ten minutes of browsing than from any checklist.

Every. Word. Counts. ▾

Your title does the recruiting

  • Use sentence case, not Title Case and never ALL CAPS
  • Be descriptive and captivating, but succinct
  • A title that hints at the finding beats one that only names the topic

Cut the text down

  • Bullet points over paragraphs
  • Avoid ALL CAPS, underlining, and italics unless they carry meaning
  • Watch spacing, alignment, and sentence length — long lines slow readers down

Use figures and tables responsibly

  • Include a figure or table only if it conveys information better than words would
  • Label everything — captions, legends, axis labels, units
  • Export at high resolution: 150–300 dpi

Keep it visual

Images attract attention and break up text. A poster that is 60% visual and 40% text will out-read one that reverses those numbers — every time.

Color, Contrast & Type ▾

Color

  • No more than two colors in the text
  • Use contrasting pairs — dark text on light, or light text on dark
  • Check accessibility with the Coblis Color Blindness Simulator
  • Avoid busy or photographic backgrounds behind text

Type & spacing

  • Body text around 24–34 pt; titles far larger
  • Don't mix too many typefaces or sizes — two families is plenty
  • White space is necessary, not wasted. Don't clutter.

Don't forget the credits. Contact information and acknowledgments belong on every poster — including your supervisor as well as sponsors and funders.

Drawing People In

The poster gets them to stop. These get them to stay.

Physical hooks

  • A hidden panel — "lift to see the result"
  • 3D models or props
  • A short hands-on demonstration
  • Handouts or a one-page summary

Digital hooks

  • QR code to the full paper or dataset
  • Short video, audio, or slideshow on a tablet
  • A live quiz or feedback poll
  • A hashtag people can post under

Where to Find Examples

Browse before you build. Find three posters you'd stop for and work out why.

Poster galleries

  • PhD Posters Gallery Broad range of disciplines, printed at real sizes.
  • F1000Research Posters Published, citable posters with DOIs.
  • ePosters Online poster journal, searchable by field.

Crowdsourced critique

  • Flickr — Pimp My Poster Drafts posted for feedback. Read the comments, not just the images.
  • Flickr — Academic Posters pool Large archive across disciplines.
  • Pinterest — Academic Posters Useful for layout and color ideas specifically.

Search #betterposter on social media for current examples of the center-finding layout, and your own conference's hashtag for what posters in your field actually look like.

Before You Submit & Getting Help

The details that vary by conference — check each one against your own call for posters.

Confirm before you design

  • Abstract deadline and how it's submitted — usually a form, often weeks before the poster itself
  • Required poster dimensions and orientation — set your canvas to these first
  • Whether the abstract appears in a printed or online program
  • Any layout, template, or logo requirements the organizers impose
  • Printing lead time — build in a buffer, and proof at full size before you send it

Writing the abstract

Four to five sentences is typical: a brief summary of the project or experience, ending in a clear thesis statement or finding.

Most importantly — communicate

Tell your program, adviser, or funding office if you need assistance or if a deadline is going to be hard for you. They can't help if they don't know you need it.

Build Your Outline

Pick your poster type, then start filling in each section — you can email or download what you write below.

Empirical Research

Data you collected or analyzed. IMRaD spine.

Non-Empirical Research

Documents, images, or a central argument.

Experiential Activities

Internship, study abroad, lived experience.

Choose a poster type above to start building your outline.

State the finding, not just the topic.

150–250 words: question, method, key finding, implication.

The gap or problem, why it matters, and your research question.

How you collected and analyzed your data.

What you found — note which figures or tables you'll use.

What the results mean, limitations, and implications.

Key sources, plus funding, advisors, and collaborators.

Your question or argument, condensed to one or two sentences.

What you're analyzing — texts, images, archival documents.

The interpretive work itself — this gets the most space on the poster.

What your analysis shows, and why it matters.

A short "read more" list, plus advisors, archives, or funding sources.

Four to five sentences summarizing the experience, ending with its goal.

Why this experience, and why now?

What you actually did — key activities, products, or deliverables.

What you learned — new skills, insight, how it shaped your goals.

Pull the main points together, and thank anyone who supported you.
